Arithmetic Sequence

SequencesCountingLogic
Game: Split the numbers into two groups and look for three evenly spaced numbers that land in the same group.
How to play: Press the small box under a number to switch it between On and Off. Choose 8 or 9 numbers to see what changes.

On — one groupOff — the other group

Play with
Look for the math

Colour nine numbers with two colours and you cannot avoid making a neat three-step pattern. Drop to eight numbers and suddenly you can. This applet lets you hunt for both.

Three numbers with the same gap

Three numbers form an arithmetic progression when the gap between the first two equals the gap between the last two: 1, 5, 9 has gap 4, and 3, 6, 9 has gap 3. Inside 1…9 there are exactly 16 such triples. The logic test lists every one of them and checks that the applet's table has no more and no fewer.

With nine, one always appears

There are 2^9 = 512 ways to switch nine boxes. Every one of them makes at least one of the 16 triples one-coloured, and the applet lights up the first one it finds. The closest any split comes is a single triple. This is the smallest case of Ramsey theory: enough objects force a pattern. The page argues this by cases; the logic test checks the conclusion directly against all 512 splits.

With eight, you can escape

Drop to eight numbers and the promise breaks. Of the 2^8 = 256 splits, exactly 6 contain no one-coloured triple. One of them is 0 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 — Off, Off, On, On, Off, Off, On, On. Try it. While eight numbers are in play the applet ignores any triple that would need number 9, and so does the core. This is why the van der Waerden number W(2, 3) is 9.

Any nine equally spaced points

The numbers 1 to 9 are only labels. Take any nine equally spaced points a, a+d, …, a+8d and give them the same two colours: the argument still forces a one-coloured triple. That is why the page says a nine-term progression split in two always has a three-term progression in one part. It also answers the colour-of-the-line puzzle: if a, a+d and a+2d share a colour, then a+d = [a + (a+2d)]/2, so two numbers and their average match. The shorter proof of that fact uses the pigeonhole principle.

Set 9 numbers and try to keep every triple mixed. Then switch to 8 and see which splits finally let you do it.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
